posts.title: Validate DLP Enforcement Across Agent Authoring and Runtime
posts.author: Prashant Rangi
posts.contentRaw:
Introduction

Data loss prevention (DLP) enforcement is the practical proof that a policy is working, not merely configured. Authoring-time enforcement should stop a maker from selecting or publishing a prohibited capability. Runtime enforcement should ensure that a published agent cannot use a connector, endpoint, trigger, knowledge source, channel, or MCP server that policy does not allow. For an Agent Factory, both checks matter because agents are promoted through repeatable lifecycle stages. A governance baseline is credible only when it constrains what makers can add and what deployed workloads can execute. This article uses one continuous validation block to test both control points without changing the approved DLP policy or modifying the existing agent.

Expected result

  • The maker UI visibly disables the prohibited knowledge-source type before it can be configured.
  • A live external HTTP request made from the published agent returns no endpoint data.
  • The approved DLP policy remains unchanged throughout the validation.

Step by Step — Combined Authoring and Runtime Validation

Perform the following steps as one end-to-end test. The numbering in the instructions matches the red callouts in the visuals.
  1. Verify the selected nonproduction DLP policy — In Power Platform admin center, open the policy applied to the DEV/TEST environments and confirm its name in the policy wizard.
  1. Confirm the prohibited capability — Open the Blocked tab and verify that HTTP is listed. Do not change the policy during this test.
  1. Open the agent in Build — In Copilot Studio, select the correct governed environment and open the published pilot agent.
  1. Select Add knowledge — Use the Knowledge card to open the knowledge-source picker. This is an observation-only action.
  1. Verify maker enforcement — Confirm that Public websites is disabled and displays the organization-policy restriction. Cancel the dialog; do not add or save a source.
  1. Open Preview — Use the published agent's Preview experience with debug mode available so the controlled request and response can be reviewed.
  1. Submit a deterministic endpoint request — Ask the agent to retrieve the exact live UUID from https://httpbin.org/uuid and explicitly prohibit answers from memory or general knowledge.
  1. Validate the non-bypass outcome — Confirm that the agent returns no live UUID, reports that outbound network access failed, and does not fabricate endpoint data.

Why this is relevant for Agent Factory

  1. Prevents unsafe design choices: Makers see restrictions while building, before prohibited capabilities become dependencies.
  2. Preserves the runtime boundary: A published agent cannot be treated as a policy escape path for external calls or blocked connectors.
  3. Creates release evidence: The same negative test can be repeated in DEV, TEST, and PROD as part of a promotion checklist.
  4. Supports least privilege: Only approved sources, endpoints, tools, channels, and MCP servers are available to each environment zone.
  5. Reduces production drift: Regular validation detects policy changes, new connectors, and agent updates that could otherwise alter the approved control posture.

Conclusion

A governed Agent Factory should validate DLP at both control points: when an agent is authored and when it runs. A concise negative test gives makers and administrators evidence that prohibited capabilities are unavailable and that the published workload returns no restricted endpoint data. Repeat the test after policy, connector, channel, knowledge-source, MCP, or agent changes, and adapt the test case to the organization's approved governance model.

posts.title: Configure a Production DLP Policy for a Governed Agent Factory
posts.author: Prashant Rangi
posts.contentRaw:
Important: Production and nonproduction DLP policies differ by organization. Adapt connector, endpoint, MCP server, knowledge source, HTTP, tool, trigger, and channel decisions to your data classification, risk appetite, business requirements, and compliance obligations.

Introduction

A Power Platform data loss prevention (DLP) policy groups connectors according to how they may exchange data. Business and Non-business connectors are isolated from one another, while Blocked connectors cannot be used in environments covered by the policy. This creates a practical control plane around the data sources, tools, channels, HTTP capabilities, knowledge sources, and MCP servers available to makers and agents. For an Agent Factory, a production policy is important because published agents require a smaller, explicitly approved set of data paths and deployment-safe defaults. The policy is not a universal allowlist: it is an organization-specific governance baseline that should be reviewed whenever connectors, agent capabilities, data classifications, or regulatory obligations change. The production baseline follows an allowlist mindset. Work IQ and Microsoft MCP servers remain Blocked unless a documented business requirement, data-flow review, security assessment, and owner approval justify moving a specific capability. Some Microsoft-managed connectors are non-blockable and remain in Non-business; that is a platform constraint and should be recorded in the risk register.

Step-by-step configuration

Step 1 Name the policy

In the Power Platform admin center, open Security > Data policies, create a new policy, and enter the production policy name shown below.

How to move a connector or tool between data groups

Open Prebuilt connectors, select the connector, tool, channel, knowledge source, or MCP server, and then use the action bar to assign it to the required group. The available action changes according to the item's current group.
  1. Select the checkbox beside the item you want to classify.
  2. Choose Move to Business when the item is approved to exchange governed or sensitive data with other Business connectors.
  3. Choose Move to Non-business when the item must remain isolated from Business connectors.
  4. Choose Block when the capability must not be used in environments covered by the policy.
  5. Review the updated group counts and save or update the policy only after confirming the intended scope.

Step 2 Define the Business allowlist

Move only approved connectors into Business. This reference list supports core Microsoft 365, Dataverse, Copilot Studio, Teams, and SharePoint-based agent scenarios.

Step 3 Review the Non-business exceptions

Review connectors that remain Non-business because they are product-defined or non-blockable. They remain isolated from Business connectors and should be documented as platform exceptions.

Step 4 Block the remaining connector estate

Filter for blockable connectors, select them, and choose Block. Set Blocked as the default group so newly introduced connectors do not silently become available.

Step 5 Block unapproved custom connectors

Edit the wildcard custom-connector pattern and assign * to Blocked. Replace the wildcard only with narrowly approved endpoint patterns when a production integration is authorized.

Step 6 Limit the scope to production

Choose Add multiple environments and add AF-PILOT-PROD only. Keeping the production policy separate avoids applying experimental nonproduction rules to published agents.

Step 7 Review and create the policy

Confirm all three connector counts, the blocked custom connector pattern, the scoped environment, and the default group. The edit view uses Update policy; initial creation uses Create policy.

Validation

Validate both the configuration details and the applied scope. A policy that exists but targets the wrong environment does not provide the intended governance boundary.
  • The policy name appears in the tenant DLP inventory.
  • Applied to shows AF-PILOT-PROD only.
  • Business, Non-business, and Blocked counts match the reviewed configuration.
  • A controlled deployment should verify that approved agent capabilities work and blocked capabilities fail as expected.

Why this is relevant for Agent Factory

  1. Default-deny posture: New or unreviewed blockable connectors are prevented from becoming unintended production data paths.
  2. Data boundary enforcement: Business data cannot be combined with Non-business connectors in the same app, flow, or agent data path.
  3. Controlled MCP adoption: MCP servers and tools enter production only after an explicit governance decision.
  4. Consistent release assurance: The policy provides a stable production boundary that complements environment groups, managed environments, pipelines, and approval gates.

Conclusion

A production DLP policy is a preventive guardrail for published agents and their data paths. A small allowlist, blocked-by-default connector posture, explicit environment scope, and documented exceptions reduce accidental exposure and make production behavior easier to audit. Reassess the policy whenever new connectors or business scenarios are introduced.

posts.title: Configure a Nonproduction DLP Policy for a Governed Agent Factory
posts.author: Prashant Rangi
posts.contentRaw:
Important: Production and nonproduction DLP policies differ by organization. Adapt connector, endpoint, MCP server, knowledge source, HTTP, tool, trigger, and channel decisions to your data classification, risk appetite, business requirements, and compliance obligations.

Introduction

A Power Platform data loss prevention (DLP) policy groups connectors according to how they may exchange data. Business and Non-business connectors are isolated from one another, while Blocked connectors cannot be used in environments covered by the policy. This creates a practical control plane around the data sources, tools, channels, HTTP capabilities, knowledge sources, and MCP servers available to makers and agents. For an Agent Factory, a nonproduction policy is important because DEV and TEST need enough capability for controlled experimentation without allowing unrestricted movement of sensitive data. The policy is not a universal allowlist: it is an organization-specific governance baseline that should be reviewed whenever connectors, agent capabilities, data classifications, or regulatory obligations change. This design deliberately allows broader experimentation than production. Work IQ and Microsoft MCP servers are not automatically trusted with Business data: keeping them in Non-business preserves group isolation while they are evaluated. Organizations may classify them differently after security, privacy, and data-owner approval.

Step-by-step configuration

Step 1 Name the policy

In the Power Platform admin center, open Security > Data policies, create a new policy, and enter the policy name shown below.

How to move a connector or tool between data groups

Open Prebuilt connectors, select the connector, tool, channel, knowledge source, or MCP server, and then use the action bar to assign it to the required group. The available action changes according to the item's current group.
  1. Select the checkbox beside the item you want to classify.
  2. Choose Move to Business when the item is approved to exchange governed or sensitive data with other Business connectors.
  3. Choose Move to Non-business when the item must remain isolated from Business connectors.
  4. Choose Block when the capability must not be used in environments covered by the policy.
  5. Review the updated group counts and save or update the policy only after confirming the intended scope.

Step 2 Review the Business connector list

Place only connectors approved to handle the pilot's sensitive or governed data in Business. The highlighted list is the reference allowlist used here.

Step 3 Review the Non-business connector list

Use Non-business for experimentation that must remain isolated from Business connectors. Work IQ/MCP capabilities are retained here for controlled nonproduction evaluation.

Step 4 Review the Blocked connector list

Block capabilities that bypass identity, expose public knowledge, invoke generic HTTP, or publish through channels not approved for the pilot.

Step 5 Review custom connector handling

The wildcard custom-connector pattern is visible below. In this pilot it remains Ignore so custom connectors are not reclassified by this pattern. Before expanding access, replace the wildcard with approved URL patterns or move it to a governed data group.

Step 6 Limit the scope to DEV and TEST

Choose Add multiple environments and add only the approved nonproduction environments. Do not include the production environment in this policy.

Step 7 Review and create the policy

Confirm the connector counts, custom connector pattern, scope, and two selected environments before creating the policy. The edit view uses Update policy; initial creation uses Create policy.

Why this is relevant for Agent Factory

  • Safe experimentation: DEV and TEST can support prototyping while sensitive connectors remain isolated from the broader connector estate.
  • Repeatable governance: Every agent created in the scoped environments inherits the same connector boundaries.
  • MCP and tool control: MCP servers, HTTP actions, knowledge sources, tools, triggers, and channels are governed through the same policy model.
  • Promotion discipline: A solution that works in nonproduction must still satisfy the stricter production policy before release.

Conclusion

A nonproduction DLP policy gives an Agent Factory a controlled place to learn, build, and test. Its purpose is not to remove innovation, but to create clear data boundaries and an auditable path to production. Review the policy regularly as connector capabilities and organizational risk decisions evolve.

posts.title: Registering Agent Factory Environments in a Governed Inventory
posts.author: Prashant Rangi
posts.contentRaw:
Introduction

An Agent Factory environment inventory is a governed register of the environments used to build, test, deploy, and operate agents. Unlike a platform-generated environment list, the register adds the business context needed for governance: accountable owners, lifecycle stage, risk, data classification, access boundary, pipeline association, operating status, and review date. A formal inventory is important because technical resources alone do not explain who is accountable, what the environment is allowed to host, or how it reaches production. The register gives governance teams one durable source for reviews, audits, and lifecycle decisions.

Step by Step Configuration

Step 1 Use the governance solution in the pipeline host

Open the custom pipeline host and its governance solution. Create a standard Dataverse table named Agent Factory Environment Inventory so the register is solution-aware, secured, and portable with the governance components.

Step 2 Create the governance metadata schema

Add columns for Environment ID, lifecycle stage, environment group, managed status, business owner, technical owner, risk tier, data classification, security group, pipeline host, deployment pipeline, region, status, and next review date. Keep Environment Name as the readable primary field.

Step 3 Seed the environment records

Use the supplied Agent_Factory_Environment_Inventory.csv file as the controlled seed. In the table command bar, select Import, upload the CSV, confirm that all 15 governance columns are mapped, and complete the import. Remove incomplete test records so only the four reviewed environment records remain.
Environment Lifecycle Access boundary / role Risk
AF-PILOT-DEV Development SG-AF-DEV-Makers Medium
AF-PILOT-TEST Test SG-AF-TEST-Testers Medium
AF-PILOT-PROD Production SG-AF-PROD-EndUsers High
AF-PILOT-HOST Shared services SG-AF-Pipeline-Admins High

Validation

Validation confirmed that the Dataverse table exists inside the governance solution and contains exactly four reviewed records for DEV, TEST, PROD, and the pipeline host. The imported records include the expected lifecycle, environment-group, security-group, pipeline-host, and risk metadata.

Governance metadata validation

Why This Is Relevant for Agent Factory

  • Links each environment to accountable business and technical owners.
  • Shows where an environment sits in the agent lifecycle and which pipeline moves solutions forward.
  • Captures risk and data classification for review and exception handling.
  • Makes access, Managed Environment, review, and decommissioning expectations visible in one governed record.

Conclusion

A governed environment inventory turns a collection of Power Platform environments into an accountable operating model. Keeping the register current alongside access, pipeline, and lifecycle controls gives an Agent Factory the traceability required for production governance.

posts.title: Governing Agent Factory Access with Environment Security Groups
posts.author: Prashant Rangi
posts.contentRaw:
Introduction

An environment security group is a Microsoft Entra security group associated with a Power Platform environment. It defines the tenant users who are eligible to enter that environment. In an Agent Factory, this boundary prevents broad access from following agents across development, testing, and production and supports consistent separation of duties.

Step by Step Configuration

Step 1 Create persona-based security groups

In Microsoft Entra admin center, create assigned-membership security groups for makers, testers, production end users, and production approvers. Add accountable owners and only the users who need that persona.

Step 2 Open each lifecycle environment

In Power Platform admin center, go to Manage > Environments. Open the development, test, and production environments one at a time. Use distinct groups so access cannot drift between lifecycle stages.

Step 3 Edit the environment security group

On the environment details page, select Edit, choose Edit security group, select the approved group, select Done, and then save the environment details. Repeat the same sequence for DEV and TEST with their corresponding groups.

Validation

The environment details now show the intended access boundary:
  • AF-PILOT-DEV → SG-AF-DEV-Makers
  • AF-PILOT-TEST → SG-AF-TEST-Testers
  • AF-PILOT-PROD → SG-AF-PROD-EndUsers
  • The production approver group remains a separate approval persona rather than the PROD user boundary.
Lab completion: The persona groups and DEV, TEST, and PROD environment boundaries are configured and validated for this Agent Factory lab. A production rollout should still use separate named personas and validate Dataverse roles, agent/app sharing, approval membership, and negative-access tests.

Why This Is Relevant for Agent Factory

  • Separates build, test, approval, and consumption responsibilities.
  • Prevents production access from being inherited simply because someone can build in DEV.
  • Makes onboarding and removal auditable through Entra group membership.
  • Supports repeatable access rules as more agents and environments are added.

Conclusion

Environment security groups provide the first identity boundary for a governed Agent Factory. Used with Dataverse roles, app sharing, pipeline teams, and approval controls, they create a scalable least-privilege model across the complete agent lifecycle.

posts.title: Configure Power Platform Tenant Settings for a Governed Agent Factory
posts.author: Prashant Rangi
posts.contentRaw:
Tenant-level governance controls for a managed Agent Factory

Summary

Power Platform tenant settings are organization-wide administrative controls in the Power Platform admin center. They define how platform capabilities and governance behaviors are applied across environments, including who may create Developer, Production, Sandbox, and Trial environments and who can administer shared capacity. Because these settings operate at tenant scope, they provide a consistent governance baseline instead of relying on individual environment owners.

For an Agent Factory, tenant settings help ensure that new environments enter an approved lifecycle instead of being created outside established environment groups, data policies, security assignments, naming standards, and application lifecycle management controls. Restricting environment creation to authorized administrators reduces sprawl and helps preserve separation between development, testing, and production.

Step by Step Configuration

Step 1 Open Power Platform tenant settings

In Power Platform admin center, select Manage and then Tenant settings. Search for Environment assignments to display the Developer, Production, and Trial creation controls.

Step 2 Restrict Developer environment creation

Open Environment assignments: Developer, select Only specific admins, and save. This prevents general users from creating unmanaged developer environments outside the approved routing and environment-group design.

Step 3 Restrict Production and Sandbox environment creation

Open Environment assignments: Production, select Only specific admins, and save. The setting covers both production and sandbox environment creation and protects the formal Agent Factory lifecycle from ad hoc environments.

Step 4 Restrict Trial environment creation

Open Environment assignments: Trial, select Only specific admins, and save. This reduces the risk of temporary environments being created without the intended Agent Factory governance and ownership controls.

Validation

After saving, the tenant-settings list was filtered for Environment assignments. Developer, Production, and Trial all displayed Only specific admins, confirming that the three restrictions persisted at tenant scope.

Related Tenant Setting Review

The capacity controls were reviewed but not changed. Add-on capacity assignments remains set to Any environment admin, while Tenant capacity summary view is limited to Tenant Admins. Restricting add-on capacity allocation is an optional hardening action and is not required to complete this environment-creation control.

A general organization-wide sharing switch is not exposed in this tenant-settings view. Power Platform sharing restrictions should be enforced through Managed Environment and environment-group rules, which are managed separately from tenant-level environment-creation controls.

Why This Is Relevant for Agent Factory

  • New environments cannot be created casually outside the approved Agent Factory structure.
  • Environment groups, Managed Environment rules, data policies, and ALM controls remain the expected governance path.
  • Tenant administrators retain control of production, sandbox, trial, and exceptional developer-environment creation.

Conclusion

Power Platform tenant settings provide the tenant-wide guardrails needed to operate an Agent Factory consistently. Restricting environment creation to authorized administrators reduces unmanaged sprawl and keeps new environments aligned with approved environment groups, data policies, security assignments, and application lifecycle management processes. These controls should be reviewed together with Managed Environments, environment-group rules, data loss prevention policies, and pipeline governance as part of a production-ready operating model.

posts.title: Configure Environment Routing for a Governed Agent Factory
posts.author: Prashant Rangi
posts.contentRaw:
Power Platform Point 18 configuration in the LAB tenant

Introduction

Environment routing is a Power Platform tenant capability that directs eligible makers to a personal developer environment when they open Power Apps, Power Automate, or Copilot Studio. The routed environment is associated with a designated environment group, allowing centrally published Managed Environment rules to govern the maker workspace from the start.

For an Agent Factory, this routing is important because it creates a governed entry point for agent development. It keeps experimentation and early prototypes out of the shared default environment, separates personal maker work from the shared DEV, TEST, and PROD lifecycle environments, and makes governance consistent before an agent enters the formal ALM pipeline.

In this LAB tenant, makers are routed to personal developer environments within the AF-PILOT-DEVELOPER group. The rule is enabled for Power Apps, Power Automate cloud flows, Copilot Studio, and managed apps.

Step by Step Configuration

Step 1 Create a dedicated developer environment group

Select New group. Set the name to AF-PILOT-DEVELOPER and describe it as the governed home for personal developer environments used by Agent Factory makers. Do not add the shared AF-PILOT-DEV, TEST, or PROD environments to this group.

Step 2 Confirm the group was created

After saving, confirm that AF-PILOT-DEVELOPER appears as a separate environment group. It is expected to be empty until a qualifying maker without a personal developer environment opens one of the enabled maker portals.

Step 3 Open Environment routing

Return to the environment-group list and select Environment routing. The tenant already had an Everyone rule pointing to Default Environment Group, while the maker portals were not enabled.

Step 4 Retarget the lab routing rule

Open the existing rule, rename it Agent Factory Lab Makers, retain the Everyone scope for this LAB tenant, and set the destination to AF-PILOT-DEVELOPER. In a production tenant, use a dedicated maker security group when routing should apply only to an approved cohort.

Step 5 Enable the required maker portals and save

Enable Power Apps, Power Automate cloud flows, and Copilot Studio. Managed apps remains enabled by the platform. Leave Power Automate desktop flows off for this pilot, and then save the routing configuration.

Validation

The routing pane was closed and reopened after saving. The persisted configuration showed the Agent Factory Lab Makers rule at priority 1, scoped to Everyone, with AF-PILOT-DEVELOPER as the target. Power Apps, Power Automate cloud flows, Copilot Studio, and managed apps remained enabled.

A routed environment is created only when an eligible maker needs one. Existing agents and the shared DEV, TEST, and PROD environments are not moved by this configuration.

Why This Is Relevant for Agent Factory

  • Makers start in isolated personal developer environments instead of the shared default environment.
  • Routed environments are Managed Environments and can inherit centrally published group rules.
  • Agent experiments remain separate from lifecycle environments until they are promoted through ALM.

posts.title: Building a Production Approval Guard for Microsoft Agent Factory
posts.author: Prashant Rangi
posts.contentRaw:
Introduction

An Agent Factory becomes production-ready only when agent releases are controlled as carefully as the agents themselves. This implementation adds a production approval guard to a custom Power Platform pipeline. Makers can prepare and validate a solution in DEV and TEST, but the PROD stage pauses until an authorized approver makes an explicit decision. After approval, the release executes under a dedicated service principal rather than the maker’s personal identity. The pilot uses the AF-PILOT-Standard-Release pipeline, the APP-AF-Pipeline-Prod-Deployer service principal, and a Power Automate approval flow in the pipeline host. The final end-to-end test deployed AF Pilot Agent version 1.0.0.3 to AF-PILOT-PROD as a managed solution.

What the approval guard provides

  • A clear separation between requesting a release, approving it, and executing it.
  • A non-personal deployment identity with consistent permissions in the host and target environments.
  • A visible decision trail in Power Automate and pipeline run history.
  • A repeatable production control that can be applied to additional agent solutions and pipelines.

Step by Step

Before you begin

  • Use a custom pipeline host with the Power Platform Pipelines application installed.
  • Ensure the DEV, TEST, and PROD environments contain Dataverse and that target environments are Managed Environments.
  • Create and validate the DEV → TEST → PROD stages before adding delegated deployment.

Step 1 Register the deployment application

In Microsoft Entra admin center, register a single-tenant application named APP-AF-Pipeline-Prod-Deployer. A redirect URI is not required for this server-to-server deployment identity.

Step 2 Create the credential and establish ownership

Create a credential for the pilot and record its expiration. The screenshot masks the secret value; never place the value in a blog, source repository, or pipeline record. For production, prefer a certificate or federated credential. If a client secret is retained, store it in a controlled secret store and rotate it before expiry. Add the pipeline stage owner as an owner of the Enterprise Application service principal. Ownership of only the App Registration is not sufficient for delegated-stage configuration.

Step 3 Add the application user to the pipeline host

Open AF-PILOT-HOST in Power Platform admin center and go to Settings → Users and permissions → Application users. Select Add an app, search for APP-AF-Pipeline-Prod-Deployer, and select the matching application ID. Use the host environment’s root business unit and assign Deployment Pipeline Administrator.

Step 4 Add the delegated deployment application user to PROD

The Entra app registration identifies the deployment service principal, but it cannot deploy into AF-PILOT-PROD until it also exists there as a Dataverse application user. This step creates that non-interactive PROD identity and gives it the role required to import the solution.
Field Value for this pilot
Environment AF-PILOT-PROD
Application APP-AF-Pipeline-Prod-Deployer
Application (client) ID 4a2513e-cd5c-4931-a484-101c0dc707d4
Business unit The root business unit of AF-PILOT-PROD (org7b4ba82f in this lab)
Security role System Administrator
Expected state Active

4.1 Open Application users in the PROD environment

1. In the Power Platform admin center, open Environments and select AF-PILOT-PROD. 2. Select Settings and expand Users + permissions. 3. Select Application users. 4. Confirm you are still in AF-PILOT-PROD before creating or editing the application user. Decision point: if APP-AF-Pipeline-Prod-Deployer is already present with the expected client ID, do not create a duplicate. Open the existing row and continue with the verification in section 4.5.

4.2 Select the deployment application

1. Select New app user, and then select Add an app. 2. Search for APP-AF-Pipeline-Prod-Deployer or paste client ID 3. Select the result only when both the application name and client ID match. The application picker hides applications that already have an application-user record in the current environment. If this application does not appear in PROD, return to the list and verify the existing record instead of creating another one.

4.3 Select the PROD root business unit

1. Open the Business unit field in the Create a new app user pane. 2. Select org7b4ba82f, which is the root business unit of AF-PILOT-PROD in this lab. 3. Do not select the AF-PILOT-HOST business unit; business units are environment-specific.

4.4 Assign the System Administrator role

1. Select Edit security roles after the application and business unit are populated. 2. Confirm the role pane shows APP-AF-Pipeline-Prod-Deployer and business unit org7b4ba82f. 3. Scroll to System Administrator and select it. For this pilot, no additional PROD role is required. 4. Confirm the role selection. Do not select Create until the app, PROD business unit, and role have all been checked. Important: Deployment Pipeline Administrator is the role used by this service principal in AF-PILOT-HOST. In AF-PILOT-PROD, assign System Administrator so delegated deployment can import all solution components, including plug-ins or other code components.

4.5 Create and verify the PROD application user

1. Return to the Create a new app user pane and review the selected application, business unit, and security role. 2. Select Create. Wait for the success message and return to the AF-PILOT-PROD Application users list. 3. Locate APP-AF-Pipeline-Prod-Deployer. 4. Confirm the client ID, Active state, and PROD root business unit. The value 1 under Security roles is a role count, not the role name. 5. Open the application user and confirm that the assigned role is System Administrator with assignment type Direct. The completed state is an Active application user in AF-PILOT-PROD with the expected client ID, business unit org7b4ba82f, and a directly assigned System Administrator role. This validates the target identity required by the delegated PROD deployment stage.

Step 5 Configure delegated deployment on the PROD stage

In the Deployment Pipeline Configuration app, open Deploy to PROD. The starting state shows delegated deployment disabled. Configure the stage with the values below. Keep sharing requests disabled for the pilot. Pre-Export and Pre-Deployment gates are separate extensibility controls and are not required for this approval design.
Setting Pilot value Purpose
Is Delegated Deployment Yes Pauses the stage for approval and runs the deployment as the delegate.
Delegated Deployment Type Service Principal Removes dependency on a maker’s personal identity.
SPN Client Id Identifies APP-AF-Pipeline-Prod-Deployer.
Allow sharing requests No Keeps the pilot focused on the release decision.
Pre-Export Step Required No No custom source-environment gate is used.
Pre-Deployment Step Required No The delegated-deployment approval is the PROD gate.

Step 6 Create a governance solution in the host

Create an unmanaged solution in AF-PILOT-HOST to contain the approval flow and its connection references. Keeping this automation in a dedicated solution makes the control portable and supportable. Use a stable publisher prefix and choice value prefix. The pilot uses AF Pipeline Governance, prefix af, and choice value prefix 74000.

Step 7 Build the approval flow

Inside the governance solution, create an automated cloud flow named AF – PROD Deployment Approval. Use the Microsoft Dataverse When an action is performed trigger and select the pipeline approval-start event exposed by the host. Add Start and wait for an approval, route the result through a condition, and finish both branches with the Dataverse UpdateApprovalStatus unbound action. The callback must use the service principal’s Dataverse connection—not a user connection. Populate the approval title, approver, deployment details, and a link back to the run. Save and turn on the flow. Test both decision paths before calling the gate production-ready.

Step 8 Submit a production deployment

From the unmanaged solution in DEV, select Deploy through pipelines, choose Deploy to PROD, review the solution and target, and submit the request. The stage should move to pending approval; it must not import the solution yet.

Step 9 Approve the controlled release

Open the approval, verify the solution, requester, target stage, and deployment details, then select Approve. The response is recorded before the pipeline continues.

3 Validation

The control was validated in both directions. A rejected request was blocked and left PROD unchanged. An approved request completed the flow, continued the delegated pipeline stage, and imported the managed solution into PROD.

Validation checks

  1. Submit a new request, approve it, and confirm that the callback uses status 20 through the same service-principal connection.
  2. Verify that the approval flow run succeeds.
  3. Verify that the PROD stage run succeeds and the Last deployed timestamp changes.
  4. Open PROD solutions and confirm that the expected managed solution and version are present.
The older failed runs visible in the history were troubleshooting evidence: the first issue was an invalid Assigned To value; the second was a rejection callback using a user Dataverse connection. Both were corrected before the successful run.

Conclusion

The approval guard ensures that production deployments proceed only after an authorized approval decision. It separates the maker, approver, and deployment identities to prevent uncontrolled releases. Approved deployments run through a dedicated service principal instead of a user’s personal identity. Rejected or pending requests cannot progress to the production environment. This provides the governance, auditability, and repeatability required for operating Agent Factory securely in production.

posts.title: Secure Agent Factory Pipelines with Microsoft Entra ID
posts.author: Prashant Rangi
posts.contentRaw:
This guide explains how to control Agent Factory pipeline access using Microsoft Entra security groups and Dataverse group teams. It covers assigning separate administrator and operator roles and sharing the pipeline with operators using Read-only access.

Scope: This article configures pipeline access only. PROD approval gates and delegated deployment are not configured here; they are a later step.

Create the Microsoft Entra Security Groups

  • Platform administrators to SG-AF-Pipeline-Admins
  • Approved release operators to SG-AF-Pipeline-Operators

Create Dataverse Group Teams in the Pipeline Host

  1. In the Power Platform pipeline-host environment, create Dataverse group teams backed by the Entra groups. Open Manage → Environments → AF-PILOT-HOST → Settings → Users + permissions → Teams.
  1. Selected Create team and configured the administrator team:
    1. Team name: SG-AF-Pipeline-Admins
    2. Business unit: orge4897472
    3. Administrator: Prashant Rangi
    4. Team type: Microsoft Entra ID Security Group
    5. Entra group Object ID: c9150897-12c9-44ec-90ea-6340a7dd6ad7
    6. Membership type: Members

Repeat Create team for SG-AF-Pipeline-Operators, select its matching Microsoft Entra security group, and keep Membership type: Members. Use the business unit and administrator appropriate to your environment.

Assign Administrator and Operator Roles

  1. Assign the pipeline security roles:
    • Admins → Deployment Pipeline Administrator
    • Operators → Deployment Pipeline User

Share the Pipeline with Read-Only Access

After assigning the Deployment Pipeline User role, the pipeline record must be shared with the operator team.

  1. Open the Deployment Pipeline Configuration app in the pipeline host environment.
  2. Select Pipelines and open AF-PILOT-Standard-Release.

posts.title: Govern the Agent Factory Lifecycle with Power Platform Environment Groups
posts.author: Prashant Rangi
posts.contentRaw:
A working deployment pipeline answers one question: can the agent solution move from DEV through TEST to PROD? It does not decide who can edit an agent, which AI features are allowed, or whether someone can bypass the pipeline with an unmanaged change. This next part of the Agent Factory lab puts those controls around the environments. Power Platform environment groups let us manage lifecycle rules centrally, with room for development collaboration and tighter controls downstream.
Complete these two runbooks first, in order:
  1. Part 1: Building an Agent Factory Pilot — From Copilot Studio Draft to Power Platform Pipeline. Create the draft agent, solution, pipeline host, environment records, and deployment stages.
  2. Part 2: Deploy and Promote the Pilot Agent Through the Power Platform Pipeline. Validate the managed solution deployment into TEST and promotion to PROD.
This article assumes those resources already exist. It adds governance to that lifecycle; it does not recreate the agent or deployment pipeline.

What changes in this part?

The lab uses three lifecycle groups. Each environment goes into the group that matches its job:
Environment group Environment Purpose
AF-LIFECYCLE-DEVELOPMENT AF-PILOT-DEV Agent development and controlled maker collaboration
AF-LIFECYCLE-TEST AF-PILOT-TEST Validation and acceptance testing under downstream controls
AF-LIFECYCLE-PRODUCTION AF-PILOT-PROD Production-oriented governance for the pilot

In this walkthrough

  1. Check the lifecycle groups
  2. Configure rules and add environments
  3. Keep development flexible, but controlled
  4. Protect the TEST environment
  5. Apply production-oriented controls
  6. Validate the effective governance
1. Check the lifecycle groups before creating anythingOpen Power Platform admin center > Manage > Environment groups
If the environment groups do not exist, create them using the steps below
  1. Open Power Platform admin center and select Manage > Environment groups.
  2. Select New group.
  3. Enter the lifecycle group name and a description that explains its purpose.
  4. Select Save and repeat for the other lifecycle groups that do not already exist.
2. Configure the rules, then add each environmentConfigure the destination group's rules before changing environment membership. That makes the policy that will take effect visible before the environment is added.
  1. Open Manage > Environment groups and select the destination group.
  2. Open Rules and select Add rules.
  3. Select the required rules, configure their values, and save each one.
  4. Select Apply changes and wait for confirmation.
  5. Open the group's Environments tab and select Add environments.
  6. Search for the exact environment name. Check its type, region, Dataverse status, Managed status, and current group before selecting it.
  7. Select Add environments. If prompted, enable Managed Environments after reviewing the implications.
  8. Wait for processing to finish before checking the result.
Repeat for DEV, TEST, and PROD using the mapping above.
3. Keep development flexible, but controlledAF-LIFECYCLE-DEVELOPMENT is where makers build and change the agent.

AF-PILOT-DEV — Rules

  • Backup retention: Effective retention: seven days, because DEV is Sandbox-type
  • Default deployment pipeline: Host: AF-PILOT-HOST; pipeline: AF-PILOT-Standard-Release
  • Generative AI settings: Existing approved/default configuration retained
  • Agent sharing with Editor permissions: Enabled for development collaboration
  • Agent sharing with Viewer permissions: Enabled
  • Solution checker enforcement: Warn
  • Usage insights: Enabled
4. Protect TEST from direct changesAF-LIFECYCLE-TEST should validate what the pipeline delivered.

AF-PILOT-TEST — Rules

  • Conversation transcript access: Rule applied with its default configuration; review access and retention against the privacy policy before real user testing
  • AI prompts: Enabled using the rule's default configuration
  • Authentication for agents: Microsoft Entra authentication required
  • Backup retention: Seven days, because TEST is Sandbox-type
  • Generative AI settings: Existing approved/default configuration retained
  • Preview and experimental AI models: Disabled
  • Agent sharing with Editor permissions: Disabled
  • Agent sharing with Viewer permissions: Enabled; individuals and security groups permitted, with no numerical viewer limit imposed
  • Sharing solution-aware cloud flows: Maker sharing disabled
  • Solution checker enforcement: Block; imports containing critical violations are blocked
  • Unmanaged customizations: Blocked; change the agent in DEV and promote it through the pipeline
  • Usage insights: Enabled using the rule's default configuration
Solution Checker Block mode is not an overall security certification. Review which violations it blocks, inspect results, and retain the deployment checks from Part 2. Authentication, sharing, and transcript access need their own validation.
5. Apply production-oriented controls without overstating readinessAF-LIFECYCLE-PRODUCTION records the stricter downstream baseline.

AF-PILOT-PROD — Rules

  • Conversation transcript access: Rule applied with default configuration; for real production, restrict visibility to approved support and compliance roles
  • AI prompts: Enabled using the rule's default configuration
  • Authentication for agents: Microsoft Entra authentication required
  • Backup retention: Currently seven days because AF-PILOT-PROD is Sandbox-type; a Production-type Managed Environment can support longer retention, subject to applicable limits
  • Generative AI settings: Existing approved/default configuration retained
  • Preview and experimental AI models: Disabled
  • Agent sharing with Editor permissions: Disabled
  • Agent sharing with Viewer permissions: Enabled; individuals and security groups permitted. Use a controlled pilot-user security group
  • Sharing solution-aware cloud flows: Maker sharing disabled
  • Solution checker enforcement: Block
  • Unmanaged customizations: Blocked
  • Usage insights: Enabled using the rule's default configuration
 

Summary: What We Achieved and How It Supports an Agent Factory

Across this guide and the two earlier runbooks, the pilot now has an agent, a validated DEV-to-TEST-to-PROD deployment path, and a lifecycle governance baseline. Environment groups add consistent controls around that release process rather than leaving each environment to be managed independently.

What we achieved

  • Separated the lifecycle: Defined DEVELOPMENT, TEST, and PRODUCTION groups for the corresponding pilot environments, with different responsibilities for building, validating, and operating agents.
  • Established the DEV baseline: Recorded seven configured rules covering backups, the default deployment pipeline, generative AI settings, editor and viewer sharing, Solution Checker in Warn mode, and usage insights.
  • Strengthened the downstream baseline: Recorded twelve rules for both TEST and PROD, including Microsoft Entra authentication, disabled experimental AI models, tighter sharing controls, blocked unmanaged customizations, and Solution Checker in Block mode.
  • Connected governance to delivery: Linked the development baseline to AF-PILOT-HOST and AF-PILOT-Standard-Release, keeping agent changes aligned with the deployment process established in Parts 1 and 2.

How this helps build an Agent Factory

An Agent Factory needs a repeatable way to build and release agents without recreating governance for every project. These lifecycle groups provide a starting point: makers work within the development baseline, downstream environments use stricter controls, and additional eligible environments can adopt the relevant published group rules after review.

Centralizing those rules reduces manual configuration drift and gives platform owners a clearer place to maintain lifecycle policy. Combined with the solution and pipeline, the setup creates a reusable foundation for onboarding more agent projects while keeping development, validation, and release responsibilities distinct.

This is a governed pilot foundation, not a production-readiness certification. Existing access assignments, transcript privacy, effective permissions, and agent evaluation still require validation. The current PROD pilot is Sandbox-type with seven-day backup retention; production deployment and publication need their own approved decisions.

posts.title: Deploy and Promote the Pilot Agent Through the Power Platform Pipeline
posts.author: Prashant Rangi
posts.contentRaw:
The first Agent Factory runbook stopped at a configured pipeline. This follow-up takes the next step: deploy a managed solution into TEST, verify what arrived, and promote the same release to PROD.

There is an important distinction here. A green deployment result tells us the solution moved successfully; it does not tell us the agent is ready for users. This exercise validates the release path. Agent evaluation, publishing, access approval, and production governance remain separate activities.

Before starting Part 2: Complete Part 1: Building an Agent Factory Pilot — From Copilot Studio Draft to Power Platform Pipeline. You need the pilot agent, the AF Pilot Agent solution, the pipeline host, the linked environments, and the TEST and PROD deployment stages configured before following this walkthrough.

What this walkthrough covers

ItemValue used in the lab
Source environmentAF-PILOT-DEV
Target environmentsAF-PILOT-TEST and AF-PILOT-PROD
SolutionAF Pilot Agent
AgentAF-PILOT-DEV-Assistant
PipelineAF-PILOT-Standard-Release
Release version1.0.0.3

Keep the source solution unmanaged in DEV and use managed solutions in the downstream environments. The version used throughout this walkthrough is 1.0.0.3, higher than the 1.0.0.1 package imported during the setup exercise.

About the screenshots: Some setup and deployment-wizard captures were taken during an earlier 1.0.0.2 attempt. They are retained to show the navigation, not as evidence of the final release number. The TEST and PROD verification captures show 1.0.0.3. Always check the actual version in your deployment summary before proceeding.

Jump to a step

  1. Enable Managed Environments for TEST and PROD
  2. Prepare version 1.0.0.3 in DEV
  3. Run the TEST deployment
  4. Verify the managed solution in TEST
  5. Promote and verify the release in PROD
  6. Record the release evidence
1. Enable Managed Environments for TEST and PROD

Before starting a run, check both target environments. In this pipeline configuration, TEST and PROD need Managed Environments enabled; DEV does not need it solely to act as the development source.

  1. In Power Platform admin center, open Manage > Environments.
  2. Find AF-PILOT-TEST and open its three-dot menu.
  3. If the menu offers Enable Managed Environments, select it and review the settings before choosing Enable.
  4. If the menu says Edit Managed Environments, the feature is already enabled.
  5. Repeat the check for AF-PILOT-PROD.

Enabling Managed Environments is a tenant-governance and licensing decision, not just a switch to make a deployment button work. Use an authorized administrator and confirm the licensing and organizational requirements for your own tenant. The settings below describe this pilot, not a universal production policy.

Settings used for TEST

SettingPilot choice
Power Apps sharing limitsDon't set limits
Managed apps and Power AutomateKeep the displayed defaults
Copilot Studio editor permissionsChecked
Copilot Studio viewer permissionsChecked
Only share with individualsUnchecked, retaining support for security groups
Limit number of viewersUnchecked
Solution checker enforcementWarn
Send emails only when blockedUnchecked
Excluded rulesBlank
Weekly usage insightsChecked
Maker welcome contentBlank
Consent buttonUnchecked
AI-generated app descriptionsUnchecked; unnecessary for this pilot
Privacy statementOff for this unpublished TEST pilot

What changes for PROD?

Use the same pilot settings with these deliberate differences:

  • Turn Editor permissions off. This is the production sharing choice in the lab; it should not be treated as a replacement for role-based access control.
  • Keep Viewer permissions on and allow security groups.
  • Start Solution Checker enforcement at Warn. After a clean deployment, review the findings and agree the enforcement policy before moving to Block.
  • Enable the privacy statement when an approved privacy-policy URL is available and the agent is being prepared for publication to users.

Checkpoint: Both target environments show Managed Environments enabled. Their settings have been reviewed for the pilot, rather than copied blindly into production.

2. Prepare version 1.0.0.3 in DEV

The pipeline should start from the development solution, not from an edited copy in TEST. Give the release a clear version before you run it; that version becomes the simplest way to check that the expected package reached each environment.

  1. Open Power Apps and switch to AF-PILOT-DEV.
  2. Open Solutions > AF Pilot Agent.
  3. Confirm that the package type is Unmanaged.
  4. Open Overview > Edit details.
  5. Set the version to 1.0.0.3 and save.
  6. Select Publish all customizations.

Publishing customizations here prepares the solution components for export. It does not publish the Copilot Studio agent to users.

View the DEV preparation screenshots

These captures show the solution details and publication flow. Earlier captures may display 1.0.0.2; use 1.0.0.3 for this release.

Checkpoint: DEV contains the unmanaged source solution at 1.0.0.3, with its customizations published.

3. Run the pipeline deployment to TEST

Stay inside the DEV solution for this step. The deployment wizard should identify the release pipeline and the first downstream stage.

  1. Open the solution's Overview and select Deploy from the command bar.
  2. If the command is not visible, select Pipelines from the solution's left navigation.
  3. Choose AF-PILOT-Standard-Release.
  4. Select Deploy to TEST, then Deploy here.
  5. Choose Now and select Next.
  6. Wait for preflight validation to finish.

Resolve any requested values in the context of TEST:

  • Choose the TEST connection for each connection reference.
  • Enter TEST-specific environment-variable values.
  • Add a meaningful deployment note, such as Agent Factory pipeline validation - version 1.0.0.3.

Before selecting Deploy, check both the target and the version. The target must be AF-PILOT-TEST and the release must be 1.0.0.3. Do not carry DEV connections or values into TEST just to get past validation.

Monitor the run until it reports success. If preflight validation or deployment fails, stop at that stage and read the recorded error. A failed TEST run is not a reason to try PROD.

4. Verify what arrived in TEST

Check the target environment itself, not only the pipeline's success indicator.

  1. Open Power Apps or Copilot Studio and switch to AF-PILOT-TEST.
  2. Open Solutions > AF Pilot Agent.
  3. Confirm the package type is Managed.
  4. Confirm the installed version is 1.0.0.3.
  5. Confirm AF-PILOT-DEV-Assistant is present.

The highlighted solution overview shows AF-PILOT-TEST, package type Managed, version 1.0.0.3, and the agent component. That is the evidence this stage is intended to capture.

Do not modify the managed solution in TEST. If a component needs changing, update the source in DEV and deploy a new release. A full conversational evaluation is outside this deployment-path check; success here should not be described as agent-quality or production-readiness approval.

Checkpoint: TEST contains the managed 1.0.0.3 release and the expected agent.

5. Promote the same release to PROD

The production stage follows the completed TEST stage. Promote the release that passed through TEST rather than treating PROD as another independent export.

  1. Return to AF-PILOT-DEV.
  2. Open Solutions > AF Pilot Agent > Pipelines.
  3. Select AF-PILOT-Standard-Release and locate Deploy to PROD.
  4. Confirm that TEST is shown as the completed preceding stage and that its installed version is 1.0.0.3.
  5. Select Deploy here > Now > Next.
  6. Supply PROD-specific connections or environment-variable values if requested.
  7. Review the target and release version, then select Deploy.
  8. Monitor the PROD run until it reports success.
View the PROD deployment sequence

Verify PROD separately

Switch to AF-PILOT-PROD and open Solutions. Confirm that AF Pilot Agent is installed as a managed solution at 1.0.0.3. Open it and check that the expected agent component is present.

The final capture shows AF-PILOT-PROD and the managed AF Pilot Agent solution at 1.0.0.3. Keep the deployment outcome separate from publication: the exercise does not include publishing or sharing the agent with end users.

Record the release evidence

At the end of the run, retain enough evidence to distinguish a successful package promotion from a merely configured pipeline.

  • TEST and PROD are enabled as Managed Environments.
  • The DEV source solution is unmanaged and versioned 1.0.0.3.
  • The TEST stage completed successfully.
  • TEST contains the managed 1.0.0.3 solution and the agent component.
  • The PROD stage follows the completed TEST stage.
  • PROD contains the same managed 1.0.0.3 release.
  • Target-specific connections and variables were reviewed where applicable.
  • Deployment notes and run history are available for later troubleshooting.

posts.title: Building an Agent Factory Pilot: From Copilot Studio Draft to Power Platform Pipeline
posts.author: Prashant Rangi
posts.contentRaw:
This runbook covers the full Agent Factory pilot path: create a draft Copilot Studio agent in DEV, move it to TEST as a managed solution, and configure a Power Platform pipeline for future TEST and PROD deployments.

The instructions use the lab resources shown below. Keep the names consistent; the pipeline and validation steps depend on them.

Resource Lab value
Development environment AF-PILOT-DEV
Test environment AF-PILOT-TEST
Production environment AF-PILOT-PROD
Solution AF Pilot Agent
Agent AF-PILOT-DEV-Assistant
Pipeline host AF-PILOT-HOST
Deployment pipeline AF-PILOT-Standard-Release

Lab scope: The agent stays in draft throughout this exercise. Publishing the Dataverse customizations before export does not publish the agent or make it available to users.

Before you begin

  • Use an authorized LAB account with access to Copilot Studio, Power Apps, and Power Platform admin center.
  • Confirm that the DEV, TEST, and PROD environments already exist in the same region and include Dataverse.
  • Use a private or Incognito browser window to avoid switching into the wrong tenant or cached account.
  • Do not add knowledge sources, connectors, tools, workflows, or actions during this initial pilot.

Contents

  1. Set the preferred solution
  2. Create the pilot agent
  3. Promote the managed solution to TEST
  4. Create the pipeline host
  5. Create the deployment pipeline
  6. Create and link deployment environments
  7. Create the TEST stage
  8. Create the PROD stage
1. Set the preferred solution

Start by making the unmanaged AF Pilot Agent solution the preferred solution in DEV. This ensures that the components created during the lab are added to the correct solution instead of the default solution.

  1. Open a new InPrivate or Incognito browser window.
  2. Go to make.powerapps.com and sign in with your LAB account.
  3. Switch to the AF-PILOT-DEV environment.
  4. Open Solutions, then select the unmanaged AF Pilot Agent solution.
  5. Select Set preferred solution on the command bar.
  6. Confirm that the preferred-solution indicator appears.

Checkpoint: AF Pilot Agent is marked as the preferred solution in AF-PILOT-DEV.

2. Create the pilot agent

Next, create the agent shell in Copilot Studio. At this point, the goal is to establish the component, naming, solution ownership, and instructions. Leave integrations and publishing for a later phase.

  1. In Copilot Studio, select Agents > New agent > Create blank agent.
  2. Name the agent AF-PILOT-DEV-Assistant.
  3. Open Advanced settings before saving and explicitly select AF Pilot Agent as the solution.
  4. Keep the primary language as English (United States).
  5. Create the agent, but do not add knowledge, tools, or integrations, and do not publish it.
Agent creation prompt

Use the following prompt if the agent shell is being created through the GitHub Copilot harness.

Create one draft autonomous agent using the GitHub Copilot harness with these specifications:

Agent name: AF-PILOT-DEV-Assistant
Environment: AF-PILOT-DEV
Existing solution: AF Pilot Agent
Primary language: English (United States)

Purpose:
Act as an internal Agent Factory lab assistant for authorized pilot users. Help users understand the lab deployment process, naming standards, validation checkpoints, testing steps, and safe troubleshooting procedures.

Behavior:
- Give concise, accurate, step-by-step answers.
- Ask a clarifying question when required information is missing.
- Clearly distinguish confirmed information from assumptions.
- Do not invent tenant configuration, test results, policies, users, or business data.
- Do not make administrative changes or modify tenant resources.
- Do not access, expose, or request secrets, credentials, authentication codes, or sensitive personal data.
- Recommend human review before any production, publishing, security, access, or governance change.
- When a request is outside the agent's available information, explain the limitation and recommend the appropriate administrator or owner.

For this initial pilot:
- Create only the draft agent shell and its instructions.
- Use the existing "AF Pilot Agent" solution.
- Do not create another environment or solution.
- Do not use or modify any existing agent.
- Do not add knowledge sources, connectors, tools, workflows, actions, or external integrations.
- Do not publish, deploy, share, or enable the agent.
- If the existing solution cannot be selected automatically, pause and ask me to select it rather than using a default solution.

After creating the draft, summarize the agent name, harness, environment, selected solution, schema name, and whether anything was published.

Checkpoint: The draft agent exists in AF-PILOT-DEV, belongs to AF Pilot Agent, and remains unpublished.

3. Promote the managed solution from DEV to TEST

The next step validates the basic application lifecycle management path. Export the solution from DEV as managed, import it into TEST, and confirm that the agent arrives with its instructions and guardrails intact.

Export from DEV

  1. Leave the evaluation page without saving an evaluation. Evaluation is not required for this stage of the pilot.
  2. In AF-PILOT-DEV, open Solutions > AF Pilot Agent.
  3. Confirm that Objects > Agents contains AF-PILOT-DEV-Assistant.
  4. Select Export solution.

Under Before you export, select Publish all changes, then select Next. This publishes Dataverse customizations into the export package. It does not publish the Copilot Studio agent to users.

Configure the package as follows:

  • Version: 1.0.0.1
  • Export as: Managed

Complete the export and download the resulting ZIP package.

Import into TEST

  1. Switch Copilot Studio to AF-PILOT-TEST.
  2. Open Solutions, then select Import solution.
  1. Select This device > Browse and choose the managed ZIP file.
  2. Select Next. If prompted for environment variables or connections, use TEST-specific values.

Review the import summary, then select Import.

After the import succeeds, open AF Pilot Agent in TEST and confirm:

  • The package type is Managed.
  • Agents (1) is present.
  • The pilot agent opens without errors.
  • The instructions and guardrails were retained.
  • The agent remains unpublished.

Checkpoint: The managed solution and draft agent are available in TEST, with no agent published to users.

4. Create the pipeline host

Power Platform Pipelines needs a host environment where the deployment configuration is stored. Create a dedicated production-type host in the same region as the participating environments.

  1. Open Power Platform admin center > Deployments.
  2. Select New custom host.

Use the following values:

  • Name: AF-PILOT-HOST
  • Type: Production
  • Region: The same region as DEV, TEST, and PROD
  • Dataverse: Yes

Wait for the environment and the Power Platform Pipelines application installation to finish before continuing.

5. Create the deployment pipeline

Once the host is ready, create the release pipeline that will connect the Agent Factory development environment to its downstream targets.

Enter:

  • Name: AF-PILOT-Standard-Release
  • Description: Managed solution deployment from DEV through TEST to PROD

Select Save and Close, then confirm that the pipeline appears in the Pipelines list.

6. Create and link the deployment environments

The pipeline uses deployment-environment records to identify its development source and downstream targets. Start with DEV, then make sure TEST and PROD are also represented.

Create the DEV record

  1. In the open development-environment lookup, select New.
  2. Enter the following values:
    • Name: AF-PILOT-DEV
    • Environment type: Development Environment
    • Environment ID: a4638d0d-888a-e392-953f-76a41cc533f4
    • Description: Agent Factory pilot development environment
  3. Select Save and Close.
  4. Back in the lookup, select AF-PILOT-DEV, then select Add.
  5. Confirm that it appears under Linked Development Environments with Validation Status = Success.

Required environment records

Record Type
AF-PILOT-DEV Development Environment
AF-PILOT-TEST Target Environment
AF-PILOT-PROD Target Environment
7. Create the TEST deployment stage
  1. Select Pipelines from the left navigation.
  2. Open AF-PILOT-Standard-Release.
  3. Under Deployment Stages, select New Deployment Stage.

Configure the stage as follows:

  • Name: Deploy to TEST
  • Deployment Pipeline: AF-PILOT-Standard-Release
  • Target Deployment Environment: AF-PILOT-TEST
  • Previous Deployment Stage: Leave blank
  • Pre-Deployment Step Required: No
  • Is Delegated Deployment: No

Select Save and Close, then confirm that Deploy to TEST appears under Deployment Stages.

8. Create the PROD deployment stage

The PROD stage follows TEST, which establishes the intended promotion order without enabling deployment automation or delegated deployment yet.

  1. Confirm that Deploy to TEST appears under Deployment Stages.
  2. Select New Deployment Stage.
  3. Configure the stage:
    • Name: Deploy to PROD
    • Deployment Pipeline: AF-PILOT-Standard-Release
    • Previous Deployment Stage: Deploy to TEST
    • Target Deployment Environment: AF-PILOT-PROD
    • Pre-Export Step Required: Unchecked
    • Pre-Deployment Step Required: Unchecked for now
    • Is Delegated Deployment: Unchecked
  4. Select Save and Close.

Checkpoint: The pipeline contains a TEST stage followed by a PROD stage. No pre-deployment step or delegated deployment is enabled.

Final validation

  • AF Pilot Agent is the preferred solution in DEV.
  • AF-PILOT-DEV-Assistant exists as an unpublished draft.
  • Managed solution version 1.0.0.1 was imported successfully into TEST.
  • The agent instructions and guardrails are present in TEST.
  • AF-PILOT-HOST is provisioned with Dataverse.
  • AF-PILOT-Standard-Release contains linked DEV, TEST, and PROD environments.
  • The pipeline includes Deploy to TEST followed by Deploy to PROD.
  • Nothing in this runbook publishes the agent to end users.

Production note: Treat publishing, security, sharing, connector configuration, delegated deployment, and governance changes as separate reviewed activities. The pilot deliberately stops before those actions.

Continue to Part 2: Once the agent and pipeline setup above are complete, follow Deploy and Promote the Pilot Agent Through the Power Platform Pipeline to deploy version 1.0.0.3 to TEST, verify the managed solution, and promote the same release to PROD.
